segments.text: The script reads raw result files and scripts. It writes two files, `S/facts.json` and `S/FACTS.md`, and it changes no other file. The comment says that every number in FACTS.md is formatted from a value that the script read or computed. The option `--print` also prints FACTS.md.
segments.heading: File comment: inputs, outputs and usage

segments.text:
Imports of the Python standard library and of `facts_data.py`.
- `sys.dont_write_bytecode = True`: Python writes no compiled copy (`.pyc` file) of the modules that are imported after this line.
- `facts_data.py` is imported under the name `fd`. The names `R`, `S` and `rel` come from it. `rel` shortens a path to the form `R/...` or `S/...`.

- `GO_LOG`, `GO2_LOG`: the logs of go.sh and go2.sh in `R`.
- `POS01`: a set of two pairs (kernel, position): `oldread` at position 0 and `asmread` at position 1. `add_bwx` (line 142) uses it as a filter for 8 earlier data sets.
- `READ3`: the kernel names `oldread`, `read` and `asmread`. Line 280 uses it as a filter for the data sets of the first runner bwx.
segments.heading: Constants

segments.text: Formats a date and time as text, for example `2026-11-17T22:12:14Z`.
segments.heading: Function `iso`: date and time as text

segments.text:
Rounds a number to 3 decimal places with the Python function `round`. For a rate that is 0.001 GB/s. `None` stays `None`.
- Two functions call it: `hw_compare_json` (line 400) and `write_json` (line 899).
- The records in memory are not rounded.
segments.heading: Function `r3`: round to 3 decimal places

segments.text: `table['boots']` is the boot list of the DIMM report, sorted by Linux start time. The function returns the last boot whose start time is not after the time `t`. The script takes this boot as the boot that ran at the time `t`.
segments.heading: Function `boot_of`: the boot at a given time

segments.text:
`D` is the dictionary that the function returns at the end. `recs` is the list of all interval records. `checks` stays empty until `run_checks` (line 653) fills it.
- `try6`: the values of `try6.txt`, the record of the boot of the rerun. `fd.read_try6` also reads the first and the last time of row 0 of `boots.txt` and of `gaps.txt`. It stops the script when row 0 of `boots.txt` does not hold the boot id of `try6.txt`.
- `bt`: the boot table of the DIMM report.
- `logs`: the lines of the two driver logs, with the state lines parsed.
- `boot72`: three fields that every record of the rerun gets. All three are read from `try6.txt`. `speed_MTps` is 7200, the speed in the line that ends with `Configured Memory Speed: 7200 MT/s`. `modules` is 12, the number in the Linux message `This system has 12 DIMM sockets`. `boot` is the boot id. The file also holds a line `modules=24`. No record field comes from that line.
- The result folders of the rerun are not read for these fields. Check `boot` (line 679) tests that every state line of the two logs and the 3 `probe.txt` files of part A hold this boot id.
segments.heading: Function `collect`: read all input files and build the records

segments.text:
Returns the fields `speed_MTps`, `modules` and `boot` for a result folder of an earlier run. `t` is the time in the folder name.
- The `assert` stops the script when `t` is not before the time until which the memory speed was 8000 MT/s. The DIMM report gives 2026-11-17 19:43 UTC for that time.
- `speed_MTps` is the speed of that line of the report, 8000 MT/s.
- `modules` is the module count of the boot that `boot_of` returns.
- `boot` is a label, for example `boot -5 of the DIMM report (Linux start 2026-11-09 21:20 UTC)`.
segments.heading: Nested function `state_of`: speed, modules and boot of an earlier folder

segments.text:
For each of the 3 entries of `fd.RERUN_A` (tags T72A1, T72A2, T72A3 with the session numbers 1, 2, 3):
- `fd.find` returns the one folder `R/k120-<tag>-<time>`. The script stops when it does not find exactly one folder.
- `fd.read_probe` reads `probe.txt` of the folder.
- `fd.read_k120` reads `threads120.csv`. It returns the processes in file order, each with its interval rows in `iv`. An interval row is a row whose column 4 (`rep`) is a number. So the `best` row and the column header row are left out [Ref1].
- No rate is computed in these lines.
segments.heading: The rerun: files of part A

segments.text:
For each of the 9 tags of `fd.RERUN_L`, `fd.RERUN_C` and `fd.RERUN_I` (T72L1 to T72L3, T72C1 to T72C4, T72I1, T72I2):
- `fd.find` returns the one folder `R/w120-<tag>-<time>`. The folder must hold exactly one csv file, and the file must hold exactly one section. If not, an `assert` stops the script.
- `sec`: the rows of the csv, read by `fd.read_bwx` and stored by kind: the T rows, the I rows, the P rows and the number of C rows. Only the T rows enter the rate. `ivs`: one entry per interval from `fd.bwx_intervals`. Its rate `total` is the sum over the T rows of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9 [Ref1].
- `session`: the second value of the entry. It is `None` for T72C4. For control I it is the number of the control process (1 or 2).
- `spec`: `cfwd` or `crev` for part C, and `like` for part L and control I.
- `env`, `launches`: the content of `env.txt` and `launches.txt`.
- `stderr.txt` is not read. Only its size in bytes is stored. Line 83 adds its path to the list `fd.OPENED` directly.
segments.heading: The rerun: files of parts L, C and control I

segments.text:
Builds the list `ev` with one entry per step: 3 sessions of part A and 9 bwx12 processes.
- Part A: `start` is the time in the folder name. `first` and `last` are the launch times of the first and the last process, from the `-- binary` header lines of `threads120.csv`. `end` is the time of the `load_after` line, which ra.sh writes into `probe.txt` after the last process [Ref10]. `load1` is the 1-minute load average of the first header line.
- bwx12 process: `first` and `last` are both the time of the `launch` line of `launches.txt`. `end` is the time of the `rc` line. `load1` is the 1-minute load average of the launch line.
- Line 99 sorts the steps by `first`.
- All these times are whole seconds.
segments.heading: The 12 steps of the rerun in time order

segments.text:
`go_start` is the time of the first state line of the go.sh log. The loop goes through the steps in time order.
- `gap_s` = `first` of this step minus `end` of the step before, in seconds. The first step has `None`.
- With the files of the rerun the gap is 5 s for the 9 steps that follow T72A1, up to T72C4. It is 287 s for T72I1 and 265 s for T72I2. facts.json lists these values under `meta.launches`.
- `state` is a sentence on the start of the step. It has four forms: the first step, a step of control I, a step after a session of part A, and a step after a bwx12 process. Example: `started 5 s after the 120-thread bwx12 process T72L1`.
- The words `idle machine` in the first two forms are fixed text. These lines do not test the load. The sentence shows the 1-minute load average of the launch. The driver go2.sh waits for a 1-minute load average below 1.0 before each step of control I.
- `D['events']` keeps the list. `evd` finds a step by its tag.

Takes a list of processes from `fd.read_k120`. `n` numbers the processes of the list from 1. `before` becomes the field `kernel_before`:
- First process of the list: the text `none (first process of the file)`.
- Later process: binary and kernel of the process before it in the list, for example `bw_old read`.
- With `order_known=False` the list holds only a part of the processes of the file. This is used for baseline A-3 only (line 198). A process whose header line is line 1 of the file gets `none (first process of the file)`. Every other process gets `not listed (other processes of the file ran in between)`.
segments.heading: Nested function `add_k120`: records of part A

segments.text:
**The rate of part A.** Each interval row of each process becomes one record. No row is left out here. No value is rounded.
- `GBps` = `iv['agg']`: column 7 (`aggregate_GBps`) of the interval row, as the binary printed it. The binary prints it with 2 decimal places (a resolution of 0.01 GB/s). The script does not compute it again. The binary computed it as the sum of the bytes of all threads divided by the longest per-thread elapsed time [Ref7].
- `rate_kind` = `fd.KIND_A`: a text that names this formula.
- `line`: the line number of the row in the csv. `interval`: column 4 (`rep`). `threads`: column 2. `passes`: column 5 (`total_bytes`) divided by column 3 (`bytes_per_thread`), as a whole number. For a read kernel that is the number of buffer passes of all threads together. The three `per_thread_..._GBps` fields: columns 8, 9 and 10.
- `stop='whole pass'` and `min_ms=500` (each timed interval lasts at least 500 ms) are constants of this line, for the rerun and for the baselines. They are not read from the csv. The `# bandwidth:` line of every such process in the csv files does hold `min_ms=500`.
- `process` = `n`. `round`, `load1_at_launch` and `launch_utc` come from the header line of the process. In a `-- step` header line (A-2, A-3) the round is the number at the end of the tag.
- `rec.update(common)` sets the fields that the caller passes, for example `dataset`. `proc_key` joins folder, file and `n` with `|`, plus the tag when the process has one.

Takes one section `sec`, that is the rows of one process. `nseq` is the number of kernels in the sequence `seq` of the csv header. `fd.bwx_intervals(sec)` gives one entry per interval. Two optional filters leave intervals out:
- `kernels`: an interval is skipped when its kernel name is not in this list.
- `positions`: an interval is skipped when the pair (kernel, position) is not in this set.
- Both filters test only the kernel name and the position. No filter tests a rate.
- Without a filter every interval becomes a record. The rerun is read without a filter (line 177).
segments.heading: Nested function `add_bwx`: records of one bwx process

segments.text:
**The rate of a bwx interval.** One record per interval that passed the filters. Nothing is rounded here.
- `GBps` = `iv['total']`. The T rows are grouped by round, position and kernel (columns 2, 3 and 4 of the row). One group is one interval. `fd.bwx_intervals` computes `bytes` / `elapsed_s` / 1e9 (columns 7 and 8) for each T row (one thread) and adds the values of all T rows of the interval [Ref1]. So the bytes of each thread are divided by the elapsed time of that thread. The unit is GB/s (GB = 1e9 bytes).
- `mesh0_GBps`, `mesh1_GBps`: the same sum over the threads on CPUs 0-63, and over the threads on CPUs 64 and above. The CPU is column 6 (`cpu`) of the T row.
- `rate_kind` = `fd.KIND_X`: a text that names this formula. The column `aggregate_GBps` of the I row is not used here. The runner computed that column with the formula of part A: the sum of the bytes of all threads divided by the longest per-thread elapsed time. Check `I-agg` (line 738) compares it with `total`.
- `line`: the line number of the I row. `interval` = round x `nseq` + position, the number of the interval in the process, counted from 0. `kernel_before`: the kernel that was timed directly before, or `none (first interval of the process)`.
- `threads`: the number of T rows.

The other fields of the record.
- `is_64_56`: the 64+56 test. `flagged`: the number of T rows with a flag. A flagged row stays in the sum.
- `stop`, `start`, `min_ms`, `count`, `thp` come from the header lines of the csv. In the 9 files of the rerun they are `common`, `common`, 6000 ms, 1 and `madvise`.
- `stop` = `common` with `min_ms` = 6000: bwx12.c sets one deadline for all threads, 6000 ms after the common start time. Each thread reads pieces of 2 MiB, and it stops after the first piece that ends at or after the deadline. Each thread reads the clock for its own start at or after the common start time. `elapsed_s` counts from that reading. So 6000 ms is not a lower limit for the elapsed time of one thread. In the 9 files of the rerun `elapsed_s` of a T row lies between 5.999979 s and 6.000457 s.
- `start` = `common` is the option `--start common` of bwx12.c: every thread starts each interval at byte 0 of its own buffer. It does not set the start time of an interval. `thp` = `madvise` says only that the runner asked Linux for 2 MiB pages for each buffer.
- `count` = 1 means that the runner was started with the option `--count`. With this option the runner reads counters for each thread and interval, and it writes the C rows.
- `rec.update(common)` sets the fields that the caller passes. `proc_key` joins folder, file and `proc_tag` with `|`.

For each part A folder `add_k120` appends the records of its 24 processes. All 6 kernels of both binaries become records, with 3 intervals each. That gives 72 records per session and 216 in total [Ref9].
- The old read kernel is the records with `binary` = `bw_old` and `kernel` = `read`. The new read kernel is the records with `binary` = `bw_new` and `kernel` = `read`. Each has 18 records: 3 sessions x 2 rounds x 3 intervals.
- Fields passed: `dataset` = `rerun-A`, `part` = `A`, `role` = `rerun`, the session number, `gap_s` and `start_state` of the step, and the three fields of `boot72`.
- `tag` is set to the folder tag, for example T72A1. `binary_sha256` is the sha256 value that `probe.txt` holds for the binary of the record.
- `gap_s` is set to `None` for processes 2 to 24. ra.sh starts them directly after the process before. `start_state` stays on all 72 records of a session. It describes the start of process 1.
segments.heading: Records of the rerun: part A

segments.text:
For each of the 9 bwx12 folders `add_bwx` is called without a filter. So every interval of every kernel becomes a record: 10 per process of part L and of control I, 6 per process of part C. That gives 30 records for part L, 24 for part C and 20 for control I [Ref9].
- Part C holds both kernels: `oldread` is the old read kernel and `read` is the new read kernel, 8 records each. The sequence of part L and of control I holds `oldread`, `asmread` and three test loops. It holds no kernel `read`.
- `dataset` = `rerun-L`, `rerun-C` or `control-I`. `role` = `rerun` for parts L and C. For control I the role says that the control was added after the first numbers were seen.
- `binary` = `bwx12` is a constant of this line. `binary_sha256` comes from the `binary` line of `env.txt`. Check `sha-bwx12` (line 768) compares it with the value in go.sh.
- `load1_at_launch` and `launch_utc` come from the `launch` line. `gap_s` and `start_state` come from the step.
- `proc_tag` is the folder tag, for example T72L1.
segments.heading: Records of the rerun: parts L, C and control I

segments.text:
Reads the three baselines of part A with `fd.read_k120`. The comment says that the rules file fixes this list.
- A-1: `threads120.csv` of the folder `R/kernels-20261113T181222Z` (24 processes).
- A-2: `A1.csv` of the folder `R/partA-20261113T205055Z` (12 processes).
- A-3: `A3.csv` of the same folder. The test `only_tags` keeps only the processes with the tag `onebuf-ms500-1`, `onebuf-ms500-2` or `onebuf-ms500-3`. The file holds 12 processes. So 9 processes are left out with all their rows.
- `A1.csv` and `A3.csv` also hold rows that start with `thread,` (the per-thread rows of the option `--per-thread`). They are not interval rows, and they give no record. `fd.read_k120` keeps their rates in `thr` of the process [Ref1].
segments.heading: The 8000 MT/s baselines of part A: files

segments.text:
`cp` is the list of all processes of the kernels `copy` and `asmcopy`, in the 3 files of the rerun and in the 3 baselines. The `assert` stops the script when the list is empty, or when the header line that the binary printed for one of them lacks the text `copy counts read+write bytes`. The reason: facts.json explains the field `passes` with this text.
- `open_probe13` (line 568) reads the other records of the 2026-11-13 run. `sha13` holds the sha256 values of its `probe.txt`, by file name.
- `D['env_partA']` is the text of `env.txt` of the A-2 folder. Check `sha-bw` (line 756) uses it.

`add_k120` appends the records of the three baselines. Every interval row of the kept processes becomes a record: 72 for A-1, 36 for A-2 and 9 for A-3 [Ref9].
- `dataset` = `A-1`, `A-2` or `A-3`. `part` = `A`. `role` = `baseline`.
- `state_of` gives `speed_MTps` = 8000, the module count and the boot label.
- `order_known` is false for A-3 only (see line 124).
- `binary_sha256` is the value of `sha13` for the binary of the record: the sha256 value in `probe.txt` of the folder `R/kernels-20261113T181222Z` (the A-1 folder). The records of A-2 and A-3 get this value too. Their own folder is not read for this field. Check `sha-bw` (line 756) tests that `env.txt` of their folder holds the same two values.
- `session`, `gap_s` and `start_state` stay `None` in these records.
segments.heading: The 8000 MT/s baselines of part A: records

segments.text:
The table `rx_sets` has one entry per data set: name, role, start of the folder name, csv files, position filter.
- 8 data sets have the filter `POS01`: L-2, L-3, L-4, R0, R0b, X1d10, X1d10b and BASEd10. Of them only `oldread` at position 0 and `asmread` at position 1 become records. Every other interval is left out.
- Example: the sequence of `p1.csv` of R0 holds `asmread` again at position 10 and `oldread` again at position 11. The intervals at these two positions are left out in both rounds of the process.
- 3 data sets have no filter (`None`): L-1, X2d12 and F72d12. Every interval of their file `a6456.csv` becomes a record.
- Only the csv files named in the table give records. Example: the folder of L-1 holds 5 csv files, and only `a6456.csv` gives records.
segments.heading: Earlier data sets of bwx12 and bwx11

segments.text:
For each data set:
- `fd.find` returns the one folder. `fd.read_env` reads its `env.txt`.
- `env['sha']` is the sha256 value of the runner binary, from the `binary` line of `env.txt`. `has_binary_line` records whether that line exists.
- The folder of R0 has no such line. r0.sh wrote none. Then the value is taken from the text of r0.sh: the 64 hexadecimal digits of the line `echo "<digits>  $BW"`. `sha_line` is the number of that line. `binary` is the path after `BW=`.
- `la`: the launch lines of `launches.txt`, by tag.
- The path of `stderr.txt` is added to `fd.OPENED`. Only the size of the file is used (line 248).

Sets `st`: the fields speed, modules and boot of the data set.
- Every data set except F72d12: `state_of(folder)` takes the values from the DIMM report.
- F72d12: `st` is a copy of `boot72`: 7200 MT/s, 12 modules, the boot id of the rerun. The folder holds no boot id. So four `assert` statements test the times of the process.
- The time in the folder name must lie after the first Linux kernel log line of this boot.
- The process must start after the time of `try6.txt` and end before the first state line of go.sh. That state line must hold the boot id of `try6.txt`.
- The process must lie inside the time range of this boot in `boots.txt` and in `gaps.txt`. These two files of the folder `R/dimm7200-20261117` hold rows with a boot number, a first time and a last time. Row 0 of `boots.txt` holds the boot id of the rerun. `gaps.txt` holds no boot id, and the script takes its row 0 as the same boot.

`D['rx'][name]` keeps the folder, `env`, the launch lines, the role, `st` and the size of `stderr.txt`. For each csv file of the data set:
- `sec` is the first section of the file. The csv files named in the table hold no `-- step` line. So each is one section. `tag` is the file name without `.csv`, for example `a6456`.
- `add_bwx` appends the records with the position filter of the data set. `dataset` is the name of the data set, and `part` is `L`.
- `binary` is the short name that `fd.SHA_NAMES` gives for the first 8 digits of the sha256 value: `bwx12` or `bwx11`.
- `load1_at_launch` and `launch_utc` come from the launch line with the same tag.
- The 11 data sets give 74 records [Ref9].

The table `step_sets` has one entry per data set: name, folder under `R`, csv file, and the start of the process tags that belong to the data set. One csv file holds several processes. Two data sets can share one file. Example: B5a and B5a-rev both read `B5.csv` of the folder `B5-20261114T011723Z`, with the tag prefixes `b5-fwd-` and `b5-rev-`.
segments.heading: Data sets of the first runner bwx

segments.text:
For each data set:
- `sha` is the sha256 value of the binary `bwx`, from the line of `env.txt` that ends with two spaces and `bwx`.
- `fd.read_bwx` returns all sections of the csv, one per `-- step` header line. `prev_step` of a section is the header of the section before it in the file. It is `None` for the first section.
- `secs` keeps only the sections whose tag starts with the prefix of the data set. The other sections of the file give no record in this data set. Example: `B7.csv` of B7a holds 48 sections, and the prefix `common-6000-` keeps 8 of them. 4 of the 8 have a tag `common-6000-offset-...`. Their processes ran with `--start offset`, and their records have `start` = `offset`.
- `D['step'][name]` keeps the folder, the file name, `sha`, `secs` and the prefix.

For each kept section `add_bwx` is called with `kernels=READ3`. So only the intervals of `oldread`, `read` and `asmread` become records. The other kernels of the sequence are left out, for example `asmread2` and `read_nop4`.
- No position filter is set. In the sequence of `B7.csv` and `C3.csv` each of the three kernels stands at two positions: `oldread` at 0 and 7, `read` at 1 and 6, `asmread` at 2 and 5. The intervals at both positions become records in both rounds of the process.
- `proc_tag` is the tag of the `-- step` line. `part` = `C`.
- `role` = `other binary (bwx)`. The two data sets whose name ends with `-rev` get the added text `, reverse kernel order, not in the list of rule V4`.
- `binary` is `bwx`, the name that `fd.SHA_NAMES` gives for `sha`. `load1_at_launch` and `launch_utc` come from the `-- step` line. `state_of` gives speed, modules and boot.
- The 8 data sets give 312 records [Ref9].

Adds five more entries to `D`. They hold no rate of the rerun, and they change no record.
- `D['hw']`, `D['hw_cmp']`: the hardware error records inside the process windows of 6 earlier data sets, and a comparison (`hw_records`, `hw_compare`).
- `D['fw']`: the saved firmware settings (`open_fw`).
- `D['a2pre']`: the run before baseline A-2 (`open_a2pre`).
- `D['mod']`: what a boot with 10 modules shows in the lines that the facts sheet uses as proof of 12 modules (`open_mod`, line 536).
Then `collect` returns `D`.
`HW_ROWS`: the 6 data sets whose processes `hw_records` tests: L-1 to L-4, R0 and R0b. All are 8000 MT/s data sets of bwx12 and bwx11 from the boot that started on 2026-11-09.

The comment gives the rule. The tests of this function use no rate.
- The journal and `launches.txt` both give whole seconds. `off` is the journal time of a record minus the launch time. So the record lies between `off` - 1 and `off` + 1 seconds after the process start.
- `inside`: this whole span lies between the start and the end of an interval.
- `possible`: the span and the interval share a part.
- `outside`: neither of the two.
segments.heading: Function `hw_records`: hardware error records inside process windows

segments.text:
`errs`: all hardware error records of the saved journal `h-5.txt`. The first `assert` requires one boot label for all 6 data sets. For each csv file of each data set:
- `la` is its launch line. The second `assert` requires that the launch lies after the start of that boot and before the `rc` time.
- `allv`: all intervals of the process, from `fd.bwx_intervals`. That call computes the rate `total` of every interval again. This includes the intervals that the filter `POS01` left out of the records. `hw_compare` (line 340) uses these rates.
- `used`: the intervals that pass `POS01`, that is `oldread` at position 0 and `asmread` at position 1.

For each record whose time lies in the process window (launch time to `rc` time, both ends included): `off` is the journal time minus the launch time, in seconds.
- The loop tests the span from `off` - 1 to `off` + 1 against each interval of `used`.
- The start and the end of an interval are the earliest thread start and the latest thread end, in seconds since the process start.
- `kind` becomes `inside` or `possible`, and `where` is the interval. A result `inside` is not replaced by a later `possible`.
- `kind` stays `outside` when the span touches no interval of `used`.

`every`: the same test against all intervals of the process, with every result `inside` or `possible` kept. `hw_compare` uses this list. Each record is stored with `offset_s`, `kind`, `interval` and `every`. The function returns one entry per process: data set, tag, folder, file, launch line, `used`, `all` and `records`.

The comment names the three result lists.
- `rows`: intervals with a record inside, and intervals that are the only one that the span of a record touches.
- `border`: records whose span touches two intervals. The resolution of 1 s cannot assign them to one interval.
- `clean`: positions at which no round has a record.
- The comment also says that this view was added after the numbers were seen, and that the facts sheet draws no wording by rule V1 point 2 from it.
segments.heading: Function `hw_compare`: an interval with a record against the other round

segments.text:
Processes without a record are skipped.
- `ivs` is the list of all intervals of the process. The `assert` requires that the rounds of the process are exactly 0 and 1.
- `mark` holds, for each interval, the records whose span touches it (`inside` or `possible`).
- The key `id(iv)` is the identity number that Python gives to the interval object.

Two nested helpers.
- `other(iv)` returns the interval with the same position and kernel in the other round. The `assert` requires exactly one such interval.
- `cmp_(iv)` returns the interval, its partner `other`, the flag `other_has_records`, and `diff`.
- `diff` = `total` of the interval minus `total` of the partner, in GB/s. `total` is the rate of an interval: the sum over its T rows.

Assigns each record of the process to one interval or to a border between two intervals. `kinds` holds one entry (`inside` or `possible`) for each interval that the span of the record touches. It must hold 1 or 2 entries.
- One entry `inside`: the record goes to that interval with `where` = `inside`.
- One entry `possible`: the `assert` requires that the span starts before the start of the interval, and that the interval is the first one of the process. `where` = `before or inside`.
- Two entries: both must be `possible`. The record lies at the border of two intervals. It goes to `by_t` under its journal time.
- `owner` holds, for each interval of the first two cases, the interval, `where` and its records. All records of one interval must have the same `where`.

Builds two of the result lists.
- `rows`: one entry per interval of `owner`. It holds the result of `cmp_`, the data set, the tag, the file, `where` and the records. `used` is true when the interval passes `POS01`.
- `border`: one entry per journal time of `by_t`. The `assert` requires that all records of that time touch the same two intervals. The entry holds the result of `cmp_` for both intervals.

`clean`: for each position, `a` is the interval of round 0 and `b` is the interval of round 1. When neither is in `mark`, one entry is added with `diff` = `total` of round 1 minus `total` of round 0, in GB/s. The function returns the three lists.

Three helpers and one value:
- `iv_`: kernel, round, position and line of an interval. `t_start_s` and `t_end_s` are rounded to 0.001 s. `GBps` is `total` rounded to 0.001 GB/s by `r3`.
- `cmp_`: the fields of `iv_` for the interval, the same for the partner under `other_round`, and `minus_other_round_GBps`. That value is `diff`, rounded to 0.001 GB/s. `diff` was formed from the unrounded rates.
- `recs_`: the journal line numbers and the distinct offsets of a list of records.
- `cmax`: the entry of `clean` with the largest absolute difference.
segments.heading: Function `hw_compare_json`: the comparison in the form of facts.json

segments.text:
Returns the dictionary that facts.json stores under `meta.hardware_error_records.all_intervals`.
- `note`: a fixed text. It says that the view was added after the numbers were seen and that the comparison is not a test.
- `with_records`: one entry per element of `rows`.
- `at_the_border_of_two_intervals`: one entry per element of `border`.
- `positions_without_records`: the number of entries of `clean`, the number of them with an absolute difference above 1.0 GB/s, and the entry with the largest absolute difference.

Reads the records of the firmware settings tool under `R`. This function reads no rate. `mtime` gives the modification time of a file in UTC, in whole seconds. The loop goes through the whole folder tree of `R`, and it collects the path of every file with the name `set.txt` or `questions.json`.
segments.heading: Function `open_fw`: saved firmware settings

segments.text:
The files that the script expects.
- `lists`: three saved lists of all settings (`questions.json`), with the keys `base`, `x1` and `revert`.
- `sets`: four files with the replies of `set` calls (`set.txt`), with the keys `x1`, `x2`, `revert` and `dimm`.
- The two `assert` statements stop the script when the files found under `R` are not exactly these 7 files.

For each of the three lists the file is parsed as JSON. Every entry must have exactly the four keys `answer`, `help`, `name` and `options`.
- `val`: the answer of the settings `TXREQ Max`, `TXREQ Min` and `DIMM Frequency`. Each name must occur exactly once. The first two are the settings that the `set.txt` files of the folder `fwtest-20261117` name.
- `unavailable`, `store_error`: the number of entries whose answer starts with `<ValueUnavailable` or with `<VStoreError`. `readable` is the number of the other entries.
- `keys`, `order`: every entry as a tuple of name, answer, options and help. `keys` is sorted. `order` keeps the file order.

Compares the lists.
- `same_entries`: true when `base` and `revert` hold the same entries after sorting.
- `same_order`: true when the two files hold the entries in the same order.
- `x1_diff`: the entries that are in only one of `x1` and `base`.

For each `set.txt`: `when` is the date and time of line 1, when line 1 has the form `Tue Nov 17 03:43:50 AM UTC 2026`. If line 1 has another form, `when` and `when_line` are `None`. `rep` will hold the replies. `block` holds a reply that is still being read.

Collects the replies. The files hold two forms.
- A line that starts with `{"responses"` is JSON. Each response gives one reply. Its kind is `set` when the response has the key `modified`, and `get` when not.
- A block that starts with `SetResponse {` or `GetResponse {` is the debug print of the tool. The first `name:` line and the first `answer:` line of the block are kept, and the value of `modified:`. The line `is_translated:` ends the block.
- Each reply holds kind, setting name, answer, `modified` and a line number.
- The `assert` requires at least one reply, and a name and an answer in every reply. `out['sets']` keeps the time, the replies, and the replies split by kind.

Reads `setting-final.txt` of the folder `R/dimm7200-20261117`. The comment of the function calls it the last reading of the memory speed setting.
- The file must hold exactly one line.
- `answer` is the text between the quotes after `answer:`.
- In the file that line is `answer: "7200 MT/s",`.

Reads the folder `R/partA-20261113T204939Z`. This function reads no rate.
- Line 1 of its `env.txt` gives the start time and the list of steps after `steps=`.
- The line `## end utc=...` gives the end time and the 1-minute load average at the end. The `assert` requires exactly one such line.
- In the file the end time is 20:50:47 UTC. The first header line of `A1.csv` of baseline A-2 gives 20:50:55 UTC. That is 8 s later.
segments.heading: Function `open_a2pre`: the run folder before baseline A-2

segments.text:
`fd.step_headers` returns the `-- step` header lines of `A5.csv` and `A6.csv`. The function stores:
- the number of header lines per file, and all header lines in `hdr`.
- `threads`: the distinct values of `--threads`. `binaries`: the distinct binaries.
- `first`, `last`: the first and the last launch time.
- In this folder the two files hold 4 and 16 header lines. All 20 processes ran `bw_new` with `--threads 1`.

Reads `launches.txt` of the same folder.
- A line that starts with `== ` belongs to one process. Its second word is the name of the csv file.
- The function stores the number of these lines and the distinct file names.
Then it returns `out`.
